title: The Language of Change
question: How do we describe *how fast* something is changing?

blocks.text: We keep saying "sluggish", "wiggly", "settles". June's right: those are vibes, not maths. I want a precise way to say *how fast* the drone is changing.
Let's replay our drone from Chapter 2 (Kp = 20 N/m) and look closely.

The {out|blue curve} is the drone's height over time. Speed is **how much the height changes per second**. On the graph, that's how *steep* the curve is at a given moment. Lay a ruler along the curve so it just touches it at one point. That ruler is the **tangent line**, and its slope is the speed.
Easy: the drone is going fastest at the very top of the bump, because that's where it's highest!
Put the cursor on the top of the bump. The tangent is **flat**. The speed is zero there!
Oh. The drone climbs, runs out of upward speed, stops for an instant at the top, and falls back. **High** and **fast** are totally different things.
The fastest moment is actually in the middle of the climb, where the curve is steepest. And when the curve goes *down*, the slope is negative: the drone is falling.
This "slope at one instant" gets a name: the **derivative**. We write it like a tiny change in height divided by the tiny time it took:

blocks.tex: \text{speed} = \frac{d\out{h}}{dt} \approx \frac{\text{change in height}}{\text{change in time}}\quad(\text{over a very short time})

blocks.text: People also write $\dot{h}$ ("h-dot") for the same thing. Same idea, less ink.
My coffee cools fast at first and then really slowly. It never quite gets to room temperature.
Because the speed of cooling depends on **how far it still has to go**. A very hot mug loses heat quickly. A barely-warm mug hardly loses any.
Let's write that down as a rule for the slope. The coffee temperature is {out|T}, the room is {sp|20 °C}:
The minus sign says "cool down when hotter than the room". The number **τ** (tau, the *time constant*) says how sluggish the mug is. For a normal mug, τ ≈ 10 minutes.
Honesty box: real mugs also lose heat by steam and radiation. This simple rule (Newton's law of cooling) is close enough to be useful.

Here's the puzzle: the rule only tells us the slope **right now**. Can we get the whole curve out of it? Let's build it by hand: look at the slope, walk along it for a little while (Δt), look at the new slope, walk again…
Twelve little steps is boring. I'll take **15-minute** steps and be done in no time.
…Wait. The coffee is at **−15 °C**?! It froze in a warm room?
The rule is fine. The *steps* are the problem. In one giant step you keep using the steep slope from the **start** of the step, long after it stopped being true. You fly right past room temperature.
We can see exactly how much. Each step multiplies the gap to room temperature by the same number:

items: Δt smaller than τ: the factor is between 0 and 1. The gap shrinks, no overshoot.
Δt between τ and 2τ: the factor is **negative**. The coffee overshoots below the room, then above, swinging back and forth while the swings shrink.
Δt bigger than 2τ: the factor is less than −1. The swings **grow** every step. Nonsense coffee.

blocks.text: That's the shower! Acting on old information too boldly makes you swing.
This is why our simulations take tiny, clever steps (1 millisecond, with a method called RK4). The swings you'll see in later chapters are real physics, not step-size accidents.
Make Δt small and switch on the smooth curve. The hand-built dots land right on it. That smooth shape is called **exponential decay**. It gets its own chapter next.
The time constant is a ruler

blocks.q: After **one** time constant, the coffee has closed 63% of the gap to room temperature. After **two** time constants, how much of the gap is closed?

options.text: 100%: the second τ closes the other 37%
options.why: Tempting, but the second τ doesn't finish the job. It closes 63% of *what's left*.
Each τ closes 63% of the remaining gap: 37% remains after one τ, and 37% of 37% ≈ 14% remains after two. So 86% is closed.
That would mean overshooting below room temperature. The real (smooth) coffee never does that. Only June's giant steps did.

blocks.text: After 1τ: 63%. After 2τ: 86%. After 3τ: 95%. It never gets *exactly* there, but after about 4–5 τ nobody can tell. Switch to the **tank**: water flowing in slows down as the tank fills, so the rule is the same ("rate depends on how far from full") and so is the shape.
So τ is a built-in ruler. Tell me τ and I know how sluggish a thing is, whether it's a mug, a tank or a drone.

items.def: The slope of a curve at one instant: how fast something changes. Written $\frac{dh}{dt}$ or $\dot h$.
Something whose rate of change depends on how far it is from where it's heading (coffee, tanks). Its curve is an exponential.
How long a first-order system takes to cover 63% of the remaining distance.

blocks.text: Slope turns height into speed. Can we go **backwards**? Suppose the drone's sensor only tells us its speed. Where is it?

If you fly at a constant 2 m/s for 3 s, you rise 6 m: speed × time. On a speed-vs-time graph that's the **area of a rectangle**. When the speed keeps changing, slice time into thin strips, treat each strip as a rectangle, and add them all up.

Sweep the cursor and watch the shaded area grow. The {out|blue curve} below is simply *the area so far*. Where the speed dips below zero (the drone falls), the area counts as **negative** and the height goes down.
The accumulated area lands exactly on the real height. Slope takes you one way, area brings you back.
This "accumulate the area" operation is called the **integral**:
That's all the integral we need for now. It comes back twice: in Chapter 7 (a transform that measures an area) and Chapter 9 (the "I" in PID piles up past error).

items: The **derivative** is the slope of a curve at one instant: how fast it's changing. High and fast are different things.
A rule like "cool faster the hotter you are" pins down the whole curve: an **exponential** approach.
The **time constant τ** is a ruler: 63% of the way after τ, 86% after 2τ, 95% after 3τ.
Building curves with steps that are too big creates fake overshoot and swings, just like the shower.
The **integral** accumulates area and undoes the derivative.

items.q: The drone is at the very **highest point** of its overshoot. What is its vertical speed?

options.why: Height and speed are different things. At the top the curve is momentarily flat.
The tangent at the top of a bump is flat: slope zero. The drone stops rising for an instant before falling back.
The fastest fall comes a bit later, where the curve drops most steeply.

items.q: Coffee at 90 °C, room at 20 °C, τ = 10 min. Roughly how hot is it after 10 minutes?

options.why: That's room temperature. It takes several time constants to get close, and it never quite arrives.
After one τ, 63% of the 70-degree gap is closed: 90 − 0.63 × 70 ≈ 46 °C.
That's exactly halfway. After one τ it's closed a bit more than half: 63%.

items.q: A drone rises at 2 m/s for 3 s, then its speed drops steadily to 0 over the next 2 s. How much height did it gain?

options.why: That's only the rectangle (first 3 s). The slowing-down part adds a triangle too.
Rectangle 2 × 3 = 6 m plus triangle ½ × 2 × 2 = 2 m. Total area 8 m.
That treats the last 2 s as if it were still at full speed. The speed was dropping, so it's a triangle, not a rectangle.

items.q: You build the coffee curve by hand with steps of Δt = 15 min, and τ = 10 min. What happens?

options.text: A slightly jagged version of the real curve
options.why: That's what happens with steps shorter than τ. At 15 min the step overshoots.

options.text: It overshoots below room temperature and swings, with shrinking swings
options.why: Each step multiplies the gap by 1 − 15/10 = −0.5: the sign flips (overshoot) and the size halves (the swings shrink).
That needs Δt > 2τ = 20 min, where the factor goes below −1.

blocks.text: Theo: "The coffee curve had a funny property: its slope was always **proportional to itself**. Is there a special function like that?"

tangent.title: Slope detective
tangent.rising: Tangent tilts up: the drone is rising.
tangent.falling: Tangent tilts down: the drone is falling (negative speed).
tangent.flat: Tangent is flat: the speed is zero right here!
tangent.help: Drag on either plot or use the slider. Each place you visit adds a point to the speed curve.
tangent.ariaTop: Drone height over 6 seconds with a tangent line at the time cursor.
tangent.ariaBottom: Speed curve, drawn point by point as the cursor visits each time.
tangent.describe: At {t} s the height is {h} m and the slope is {v} m per second.

coffee.title: Build the coffee curve by hand
coffee.aria: Coffee temperature built step by step. Each step follows the current slope for one step size. The dashed orange line previews the next step.

status.start: The coffee starts at 90 °C, cooling at {r} °C per minute. The orange dashes show where one step will land.
status.step: Step {n}: at {t} min the coffee is {T} °C, cooling at {r} °C per minute.
status.frozen: Wait… {T} °C? The coffee got colder than the room!
status.growing: And the swings are getting bigger!
status.dipped: (On the way it dipped below room temperature!)

ruler.title: The time-constant ruler
ruler.aria: Exponential curve with vertical marks at one, two and three time constants, labelled 63, 86 and 95 percent.
ruler.describe: Time constant {tau} minutes. Marks at one, two and three time constants show 63, 86 and 95 percent of the way.

area.title: Adding up area
area.start: Press play (or drag) to start adding up strips.
area.positive: Speed above zero: each strip adds height.
area.negative: Speed below zero: these strips count as negative. The height goes down.
area.ariaTop: Drone speed over time with the area under the curve shaded up to the cursor.
area.ariaBottom: The accumulated area plotted over time, on top of the real height curve.
area.describe: Up to {t} s the accumulated area is {a} metres.
